name: Beth Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the pig unit at Harrow's, about four hundred sows, and the family grows wheat and barley too, mostly to feed the pigs. I'm in the farrowing house, where the sows have their piglets. Start at six, check every crate, every litter, pull out any piglet that's been lain on, top up the feed, wash down. At harvest they put me on the grain cart as well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good farrowing, honestly. A sow with fourteen piglets all lined up feeding, that's a lovely thing to see first thing. What wears me out is losing them. You find a dead piglet most mornings, and some days four or five. Philip, the boss, says you get used to it. I haven't yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI or computer tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've got a phone for calls and messages and that's it. The unit has a computer that controls the feed and the heat lamps, but Philip's son Matt sees to that. I write my notes on the whiteboard in the office, same as Philip's dad did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, keep it that way. We don't need it on a pig farm. Pigs need people who turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things stay as they are, which suits me. I'm not on much, and me and Daniel have maybe three weeks of money put by, but we're getting married next September and we'll manage. My nan brought up five on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the job properly, that's my whole plan. Philip says another year and I can do the injections and the castrating on my own. And keep going to chapel on Sundays and save what we can for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. This one feels right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it you still need to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading a sow. When she's about to farrow, when she's off, when she's going to turn on her piglets. Philip just looks over the crate and knows. I've been there two years and I'm still guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your nan. What did she teach you about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't owe anyone. If you can't pay cash, you don't have it. Daniel's mum says get a loan for the wedding and I won't. We'll do it in the chapel hall with sandwiches if we have to.

S0.say: I'd say keep it that way, because a pig farm doesn't need AI. Pigs need people who turn up.
S0.think: It means things stay as they are, which suits me. Daniel and I have about three weeks of money, we marry next September, and we'll manage like my nan did.
S0.do: Keeps learning the job so she can give injections and castrate piglets on her own within a year. Goes to chapel on Sundays and saves what she can for the wedding, refusing to borrow.
S0.feel: Calm and settled. This scenario feels right to her.
S0.quote: Pigs need people who turn up.
S0.fieldNote: Firm, short opinions and a strong sense of family example; her grandmother's rule about debt shapes everything. She's honest that she is still guessing after two years. Faith and the wedding set the rhythm of her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's wrong. Young people need to be taken on and taught, that's how it's always worked. Apprenticeships, not computers. I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry for my cousin Lily. She's sixteen and wants to work with pigs, and if farms stop taking beginners she'll end up in a shop. For me, I'm in, but I'm still the junior. If something goes, it's the junior's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and work. Ask Philip if he'd take Lily for the summer, even unpaid at first, so she gets her foot in. Not change anything I do myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Lily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the unit's computer, so you're less junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Matt does that. I'd be useless at it and slow everyone down. I'm better spending the time with the sows. That's what I'm there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would be behind fewer beginners being hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies who've never mucked out a shed. People in cities who think food comes from a lorry. Not Philip. Philip took me on when nobody else would, with no experience.

S1.say: I'd say it's wrong, because young people need to be taken on and taught, the way it's always worked. Apprenticeships, not computers.
S1.think: I worry for my cousin Lily, who is sixteen and wants to work with pigs. I'm in, but I'm still the junior, and if something goes it's the junior's jobs.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and asks Philip to take Lily on for the summer, unpaid at first if necessary. Doesn't change anything about her own work or learn the unit's computer.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for her young cousin.
S1.quote: Big companies who've never mucked out a shed. People in cities who think food comes from a lorry.
S1.fieldNote: Her first concern was family, not herself. She refused to learn the unit's computer, firmly and without apology. She blames distant companies and city people, never her own employer, who she feels loyal to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not my world. People in offices will have to find other work, same as farmers have had to for a hundred years. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it does touch us. Daniel works at the feed mill, mostly driving the loader, but he does the delivery paperwork in the afternoons. If a computer does all that, they'll cut his afternoons. He's only just got them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell Daniel to get his lorry licence, so he's driving, not typing. We'd hold off on the car we were going to buy after the wedding. I'd pray on it, honestly. That's what I do when I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Bit worried for Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want the government paying people to sit at home. What would you want them to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help them get a trade. Pay a farm or a builder to take them on and teach them. That's a hand up. A cheque every month just makes people soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Daniel feel about you suggesting the lorry licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then he'd do it. He likes being told what to do, I think, he just won't say it. His dad drove lorries, so it wouldn't feel strange to him.

S2.say: I'd say it's not my world, and office workers will have to find other work like farmers have for a hundred years. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home.
S2.think: It does touch us, because Daniel does the feed mill's delivery paperwork in the afternoons. If a computer does that, his afternoon hours go.
S2.do: Pushes Daniel to get his lorry licence so he's driving rather than typing. Delays buying a car after the wedding, and prays about it.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with a worry centred on Daniel.
S2.quote: That's a hand up. A cheque every month just makes people soft.
S2.fieldNote: Her public line was hard on office workers, but privately the threat reached her fiancé's paperwork hours. Her policy answer was clear and in character: pay employers to train people, no regular payments. Prayer came up naturally as her way of handling uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's about time people respected hands-on work. Everyone's always looked down on farm workers. Now they'll see who's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But off the record, I don't trust where the money goes. If shares boom, it's the rich getting richer, and they'll buy up farms as investments. A man in a suit owns the land and sends in someone to cut costs. That's what frightens me, not the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hold on. Get the wedding done. Maybe ask Philip whether there's a cottage on the farm we could rent, because if house prices go up, we're never getting a place of our own. Tell Lily to stick with the pigs, because that's safe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Proud, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good, people will respect hands-on work, and also that you're frightened. Which is closer to the truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'd feel proud and I'd feel scared. Proud of the work. Scared of who ends up owning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your church friends about the political crisis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to pray for whoever's in charge, because they'll get it wrong whatever they do. And that the people who get rich should give something back of their own will, not be forced. That's how it should work.

S3.say: I'd say it's about time people respected hands-on work, since farm workers have always been looked down on. Now they'll see who's needed.
S3.think: I don't trust where the money goes. If shares boom, rich investors buy farms and send in someone to cut costs, and that frightens me more than AI.
S3.do: Gets the wedding done and asks Philip about renting a cottage on the farm, since house prices would rule out buying. Tells her cousin to stay with pig work.
S3.feel: Proud of hands-on work but anxious about who will own it.
S3.quote: Proud of the work. Scared of who ends up owning it.
S3.fieldNote: A clear say and think gap: public pride, private fear of outside investors buying farms. She favours voluntary giving over forced redistribution, in line with her outlook. Asked to choose, she held both feelings and said so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it won't work. Pigs aren't boxes. Anyone who's worked a farrowing house knows that. I'd say that to the papers if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. They've already got cameras that can count piglets and robots that wash out pens. A sow knows my voice. You can't tell me a machine walking up the farrowing house is the same thing, and if it is, God help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd do. Stay as long as Philip keeps me. Not learn the robots, I couldn't. If I lost the job, I'd look at the care home in town, if that's not robots too, or the school kitchen. Pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the ground's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel the night Philip told you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be fine, the Lord provides, and then I'd cry in the bathroom so he didn't see. Then in the morning I'd go back and do my shift properly, because I'd want Philip to remember I did it right to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you willing to learn to run the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Philip asked me himself and said he needed me, I'd try. For him, not for the machine. But I'd be bad at it. I can't even get the new phone to do what I want.

S4.say: I'd say robots are wrong and won't work, because pigs aren't boxes, and anyone who's worked a farrowing house knows it. I'd say that to the papers.
S4.think: I'm frightened, because cameras that count piglets and robots that wash out pens already exist. A sow knows my voice, and a machine walking the farrowing house isn't the same thing.
S4.do: Stays as long as Philip keeps her and won't try to learn the robots unless he personally asks. Looks at the care home or school kitchen in town if the job goes, and prays about it.
S4.feel: Frightened, as if the ground is going.
S4.quote: A sow knows my voice. You can't tell me a machine walking up the farrowing house is the same thing, and if it is, God help us.
S4.fieldNote: Her loyalty to her boss would outweigh her resistance to technology, but only if he asked her himself. The picture of crying in the bathroom and then doing her shift properly to the end said a lot about her pride. Her fear was the most open of anything she said.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots. That's the one where I've got nothing to offer. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, where farms get paid to keep young people on and teach them, even with robots. And keep family farms in family hands, not sold to investors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. Nobody asks if a sow is happier with a person or a machine. I think I know the answer, but I'd want someone to ask.

headlineQuote: A sow knows my voice. You can't tell me a machine walking up the farrowing house is the same thing, and if it is, God help us.
portrait: Beth Baker is a 27-year-old junior in the farrowing house of a 400-sow pig farm, still learning to read a sow after two years. She never uses AI tools, goes to chapel on Sundays and is saving with her fiancé Daniel, who works at the feed mill, for a wedding they refuse to borrow for. Across the scenarios she worries first for family, her young cousin Lily and Daniel's paperwork hours. She blames distant companies, city people and outside investors rather than her boss, to whom she is fiercely loyal. With robots she is frightened and can't see herself learning them, and what she wants is real apprenticeships and family farms kept in family hands.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because it's the one where she feels she has nothing to offer.
whatWouldHelp: Real apprenticeships where farms are paid to keep and teach young people, and keeping family farms out of investors' hands.
